law-01.title: NPPL Microlight — what it is
law-01.body:
NPPL Microlight — UK national licence

The National Private Pilot’s Licence (NPPL) is a UK-specific licence. It is not automatically recognised abroad. With a Microlight Class Rating you may fly microlights under the privileges of that rating.

To get an NPPL with Microlight Class Rating you train with a UK CAA-certificated flight instructor entitled to instruct on microlights, pass the ground exams, and pass a General Skills Test (GST) plus type oral with an authorised examiner.

Hours (Without Operational Limitations) — typically: minimum 25 hours total under instruction, 10 solo, 5 navigation (of which 3 solo nav). Confirm current BMAA / CAP figures with your instructor.
With Operational Limitations — lower hour minima, but initially: no passengers, cloud base not less than 1,000 ft AGL, visibility not less than 10 km, and not further than 8 NM from take-off.
  • Minimum ages (typical teaching): solo from 16, licence from 17 — confirm current ANO.
  • Ground exams in five theory subjects must be passed within 24 months before licence application.
  • GST and oral typically within 9 months before application.
Confirm all currency, hour and age figures with your instructor and the current official syllabus / CAP 3181.

law-02.title: UK airspace classes & VFR
law-02.body:
UK airspace for microlight VFR

In the UK you fly under SERA and UK differences published in the AIP. Microlights like the C42 typically operate day VFR.

  • Class A — no VFR. Example context: London TMA above many Home Counties fields is Class A. Stay out unless you have an IFR clearance (microlight NPPL does not give you that).
  • Class D CTR/CTA — need an ATC clearance before entry.
  • Class G — uncontrolled; you still obey SERA VMC minima and Rules of the Air.

Day VMC minima (remember the tight box)

Low-level Class G teaching points often used for light aircraft/microlights: at or below 3,000 ft AMSL, IAS ≤140 kt — typically 1,500 m flight visibility, clear of cloud and with the surface in sight. Above 3,000 ft the “5 km / 1,500 m horizontal / 1,000 ft vertical from cloud” picture applies.

Ops-limits NPPL weather (10 km / 1,000 ft AGL cloud) is tighter than SERA. Stay in the tighter box until limitations are lifted.
Exact SERA.5001 figures and UK differences: confirm with current AIP ENR 1.2 / instructor.

law-03.title: ATZ, MATZ, low flying & right of way
law-03.body:
ATZ, MATZ and see-and-avoid

An Aerodrome Traffic Zone (ATZ) protects the circuit. Rough teaching size: for a runway ≤1,850 m, a circle of 2 NM radius from the midpoint up to 2,000 ft above aerodrome level. Rule 11: establish two-way communications before entering (or follow the published procedure).

A MATZ (Military Aerodrome Traffic Zone) is not civil controlled airspace, but good airmanship is to call for penetration. The civil ATZ inside still needs proper two-way — do not bust it.

Low flying (UK teaching points)

  • Congested areas: typically not below 1,000 ft above the highest fixed object within 600 m.
  • Elsewhere: not within 500 ft of any person, vessel, vehicle or structure (with training/exceptions as taught).

Right of way (basics)

  • Converging: give way to the other on your right.
  • Head-on: both alter right.
  • Overtaking: pass on the right; the one being overtaken has right of way.
  • Landing aircraft / gliders generally have priority as taught — gliders win in many conflict pictures.
Confirm Rule numbers and exact wording in current Rules of the Air / SERA with your instructor.

law-04.title: Documents, alcohol, squawks & incidents
law-04.body:
PIC responsibilities

You decide go/no-go. Legal VFR can still be a poor day for a light microlight (gusty crosswind, CB nearby).

  • Be able to produce licence + medical/PMD, Certificate of Registration, and Permit to Fly / Certificate of Validity when required.
  • Passenger currency teaching point: 3 take-offs and landings in the preceding 90 days as PIC before carrying passengers.
  • Alcohol limits (UK): 20 mg/100 ml blood, 9 µg/100 ml breath, 27 mg/100 ml urine. Practice: many schools teach “8 hours bottle to throttle” and longer after a heavy night.

SSR codes (know cold)

  • 7000 — VFR conspicuity
  • 7700 — emergency · 7600 — radio fail · 7500 — unlawful interference
  • 0030 — FIR lost (when appropriate)
  • 121.500 MHz — guard / D&D

Accidents → AAIB (+ police as required). MOR within timescales taught. AIRPROX → UKAB.

Local listening squawks (e.g. field-specific codes) change — check current AIP / Skyway / plate.

tech-01.title: Four forces & aerofoil
tech-01.body:
Lift, weight, thrust, drag

In steady level flight the four forces balance. An aerofoil produces lift mainly because air over the upper surface moves faster → lower pressure (Bernoulli) plus the wing deflects air downward (Newton).

Angle of attack (AoA) is the angle between the chord line and the relative airflow. Increase AoA → more lift (and drag) until the stall angle, when the smooth flow breaks down and lift drops sharply.

A microlight like the C42 is light and low-inertia — gusts and turbulence hit harder than in a heavier training aeroplane. Fly ahead of the aircraft.
  • Stall speed rises with weight, load factor (bank), and centre of gravity changes.
  • In a level 60° bank turn, load factor is 2g — stall speed rises by about √2 ≈ 1.41.

tech-02.title: Engine, fuel & carb ice (Rotax context)
tech-02.body:
Microlight powerplant — Rotax 912 context

Many UK microlights (including C42 variants) use a Rotax 912 series: four-stroke, dual carburettor, reduction gearbox. Exact RPM, oil and coolant limits are in your POH / TADS — memorise the placard, not a mate’s numbers.

  • Fuel: often MOGAS (min grade on placard), UL91, or AVGAS 100LL — prolonged AVGAS may not be ideal for some Rotax fits; follow the POH.
  • Carburettor icing: the venturi can be tens of degrees colder than OAT. Risk exists even on mild UK days at low power.
  • Some C42 variants have carb heat; others may not — check the actual knob/airframe you fly.
Carbon monoxide: colourless and odourless. Exhaust + cabin heat is a classic risk. Active detector preferred; heat OFF, fresh air, land if alerted.
Type-specific performance numbers: use your weighing report, placard and current TADS/POH — do not invent figures.

tech-03.title: Airspeeds, flaps & weight & balance
tech-03.body:
V-speeds and loading (teaching picture)

Know what the symbols mean; then learn your numbers from the POH.

  • Vs0 / Vs1 — stall flaps landing config / clean
  • Vne — never exceed
  • Va — manoeuvring / max turbulent-air speed (roughly)
  • Vfe — max flap extended

Weight & balance: empty mass from last weighing + crew + bags + fuel mass must be ≤ MTOW, with CG inside limits. Fuel has mass (petrol ≈ 0.72 kg/L is a common planning figure).

UK microlights fly on a Permit to Fly with Certificate of Validity, not a full Certificate of Airworthiness. Daily inspection is on you as PIC.
C42 MTOW/CG/V-speeds vary by variant (e.g. Bravo differences training if MTOW > 475 kg). Confirm with instructor / TADS.

tech-04.title: Walk-round & systems checklist mindset
tech-04.body:
Daily inspection that matters

  • Fuel: quantity seen with your eyes, cap secure, drains sampled, correct type.
  • Oil and coolant levels; cowl secure; propeller free of nicks.
  • Flying surfaces, hinges, control horns, free movement, trim.
  • Undercarriage, tyres, brakes as fitted.
  • Doors, pins, harnesses; ballistic parachute handle if fitted — know the placard.
  • Controls full and free; instruments; radio/transponder; mag check per checklist.

Engine failure after take-off: lower the nose to best glide (POH), pick a field early. Microlight engines are not “certificated transport category” — always keep an option.

met-01.title: ISA, pressure & altimetry (UK)
met-01.body:
International Standard Atmosphere & UK altimeter settings

  • ISA sea level: 15 °C, 1013.25 hPa, density 1.225 kg/m³.
  • ISA temperature lapse ≈ 2 °C per 1,000 ft.
  • QNH — altimeter reads altitude above mean sea level when on the ground at that aerodrome.
  • QFE — altimeter reads height above the aerodrome elevation (often used in UK circuits).
  • 1 hPa ≈ 27–30 ft. If QNH falls and you do not reset, you are lower than the altimeter suggests.
Cold air: true altitude is lower than indicated (~4 ft per 1,000 ft per 1 °C below ISA is a common teaching rule of thumb).
Transition altitude and local procedures: UK AIP ENR 1.7 and aerodrome plate. Under London TMA use aerodrome QNH as taught — confirm with instructor.

met-02.title: Wind, clouds & UK air masses
met-02.body:
Wind and cloud for microlight decisions

Surface wind is usually backed and slower than the wind at 2,000 ft (friction). In the Northern Hemisphere, Buys Ballot: back to the wind, low pressure on the left.

Know your personal / school surface and crosswind limits. Gusts count. METAR “G” typically when gust ≥10 kt above the mean.

  • ST stratus — sheet, poor vis, can sit on hills.
  • CU/SC — often workable if base is high enough with gaps.
  • TCU/CB — no for a microlight: turbulence, lightning, hail, gust fronts.
  • NS — warm-front rain sheet; base and vis drop.

UK air masses (simple): maritime tropical (warm, moist, drizzle); maritime polar (showers, good vis between); continental polar (cold, clear, radiation fog risk).

met-03.title: Fronts, fog, icing & carb ice
met-03.body:
Fronts and go / no-go hazards

  • Warm front: cloud sequence CI→CS→AS→NS; rain; poor vis; wind backs then veers.
  • Cold front: line of CU/CB; sharp showers; clearer cooler air behind; wind veers.
  • Occlusion: treat as prolonged weather — do not squeeze a microlight through.

Fog: FG visibility <1,000 m; BR 1,000–5,000 m. Radiation fog: clear night, inland, light wind. Hill fog on ridges (e.g. Chilterns teaching context).

Icing: many microlights have no known-icing approval. Cloud near 0 °C → turn around. Carb ice can form with cool moist air even when OAT looks “fine”.

Any thunderstorm nearby: stay on the ground. Gust front can arrive before the rain.

met-04.title: METAR, TAF & UK briefing
met-04.body:
Decode enough to decide

  • Wind: 24012KT = from 240° true at 12 kt. 25021G31KT = 21 gusting 31 — often a microlight no-go.
  • Visibility 9999 = 10 km or more. Cloud: FEW/SCT/BKN/OVC with height in hundreds of feet AAL (SCT036 = 3,600 ft).
  • CAVOK: ≥10 km, no cloud below 5,000 ft or MSA, no CB/TCU, no significant weather.
  • TEMPO = temporary periods; BECMG = lasting change; PROB30 = plan as if it might happen.
  • Q1005 = QNH 1005 hPa. Temp/dewpoint close at dusk → watch fog.

Use Met Office aviation products / F214–F215 style charts as taught, plus nearby METARs/TAFs. Forecasts go stale — re-check in the last hour before flight.

Briefing portals change over time — use the current UK authorised source your school recommends.

hpl-01.title: IMSAFE & fitness to fly
hpl-01.body:
IMSAFE — before you drive to the airfield

  • I Illness — cold, sinus, blocked ears. Cannot clear ears = do not fly.
  • M Medication — drowsy antihistamines/codeine mixes are a no. New meds: days on the ground. Confirm with AME/instructor lists.
  • S Stress — steals spare capacity.
  • A Alcohol — legal limits are low; practice bottle-to-throttle discipline.
  • F Fatigue — aim for proper sleep; tired pilots bust CAS.
  • E Eating — low blood sugar looks like poor flying; hydrate.
A Pilot Medical Declaration (PMD) is not a daily warrant. If you feel unfit, you are unfit.

hpl-02.title: Vision, balance & illusions
hpl-02.body:
Eyes, ears and the leans

Scan in chunks (about ≤10° hops), covering well left and right of track. Empty-field myopia over haze — refocus on a wingtip. High-wing: lift a wing before turning to clear the blind spot.

  • Sunglasses: grey/brown; avoid polarised (LCD/canopy issues) and beware photochromic lenses that stay light under canopy.
  • The leans: slow unnoticed bank, then roll-out feels wrong — trust the visual horizon.
  • Somatogravic illusion: acceleration feels like a climb — do not push the nose down after take-off based on “seat of the pants” alone.

Motion sickness: look at the horizon, cool air, avoid heads-down map study in bumps; cut the sortie short if needed.

hpl-03.title: CO, hypoxia & hyperventilation
hpl-03.body:
Gases — CO is the practical microlight killer

Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin. Rotax exhaust + cabin heat is the classic scenario. Symptoms: headache, flu-like, poor judgement. Action: heat OFF, max fresh air, land, do not take off with an alert that will not clear.

Hypoxia teaching altitudes are often above where a typical C42 operates day-to-day, but the exam still asks oxygen rules. CO creates an anaemia-like hypoxia even at circuit height.

Hyperventilation at height: treat as hypoxia and descend. On the ground it is often stress — slow the breathing and fly the aircraft.

hpl-04.title: Hazardous attitudes & personal minima
hpl-04.body:
Aeronautical decision-making

Hazardous attitudes (as commonly taught from CAP material): anti-authority, impulsiveness, invulnerability, macho, resignation (plus peer pressure in many briefings). Name it, then pick the boring safe option.

Startle (engine cough, conflicting traffic, CO alarm): skilled performance can wobble for several seconds. Aviate → Navigate → Communicate.

Personal minima should beat legal minima. 1,500 m visibility may be legal in low Class G and still be a terrible microlight afternoon.

If you would not take a friend, do not take yourself. Drive home.

nav-01.title: Track, heading, variation & 1-in-60
nav-01.body:
The navigation words

  • Track — path over the ground (what you drew).
  • Heading — where the nose points (track ± drift).
  • Drift — wind from the left → heading a little left (into wind) to stay on track.
  • TVMDC — True → Variation → Magnetic → Deviation → Compass. Easterly variation: magnetic is smaller than true (“East is least”).

1-in-60 rule: 1° off at 60 NM ≈ 1 NM off track. Track error ° ≈ (distance off ÷ distance gone) × 60.

Mental maths: 90 kt ≈ 1.5 NM/min. Time (min) = distance × 60 / groundspeed.

nav-02.title: UK charts, NOTAMs & altimeter choice
nav-02.body:
Half-mil and quarter-mil

  • 1:500,000 (half mil): 1 NM ≈ 3.7 mm. Best for CAS picture.
  • 1:250,000: more ground detail; check what airspace it omits — confirm legend.

Measure tracks from the nearest meridian. Use a current chart edition. NOTAMs every flight from NATS AIS — RA(T), gliding, U/S A/G, royal flights. Graphical filters miss things.

Under busy TMA airspace, aerodrome QNH is usually preferred over Regional Pressure Setting as taught for that area — confirm ENR 1.7 / instructor.

Chart symbols and airspace fills: NATS VFR legend + current AIP win.

nav-03.title: Fuel planning & safety altitude
nav-03.body:
Fuel and MSA mindset

Plan taxi + trip + diversion + a safe reserve. For UK microlight Permit ops, follow ANO fuel requirements as taught; many schools use ~30 minutes cruise fuel as a practical day-VFR margin (align with your instructor / NCO AMC teaching).

See fuel in the tank — do not trust a sender alone. Safety altitude: highest terrain/obstacles near the route + a margin. Chart MEF is not automatically your safety altitude. CAS bases may be the limiting ceiling.

GPS is a tool. Chart + stopwatch + lookout is the skill. When the tablet overheats, you still have to get home.

nav-04.title: Lost procedures (UK)
nav-04.body:
Unsure of position

  1. Aviate — stay VMC.
  2. Confess early.
  3. Climb if it helps radio/view — but watch controlled airspace above you.
  4. Communicate: working ATSU first, else 121.500.
  5. Squawk 0030 if appropriate when on conspicuity and unsure.

If following a line feature, UK airmanship teaching is often to keep the feature on your left (fly to the right of it). Confirm current advice with instructor.

If weather on the nose is worse than the plan, the next turning point is a field — not “maybe it improves”.

radio-01.title: FRTOL basics, phonetics & readbacks
radio-01.body:
UK Flight Radiotelephony (FRTOL)

An aircraft radio station licence covers the set; you need an FRTOL (or be a student under instruction) to operate the COM. CAP 413 is the UK phraseology bible; Skyway Code helps with practical UK GA.

  • First callsign: always full phonetic (e.g. Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta). Only shorten after ATC/ATS shortens you.
  • Solo student: prefix STUDENT on first contact with an ATSU.
  • Station suffix tells the job: RADIO (A/G), INFORMATION (AFIS), TOWER/GROUND/APPROACH (ATC — can clear), TRAFFIC (unmanned).

Words that matter

  • AFFIRM / NEGATIVE — yes / no.
  • ROGER — received. Does not mean you will comply.
  • WILCO — understood and will comply.
  • CLEARED — only ATC says this.
Mandatory full readbacks include: taxi; level; heading; runway in use; enter/land/take-off/backtrack/cross/hold short; SSR code; altimeter; frequency change; type of ATS service — see current CAP 413 list.
radio-01.speakExtra: Alpha Bravo Charlie Delta Echo Foxtrot Golf Hotel India Juliett Kilo Lima Mike November Oscar Papa Quebec Romeo Sierra Tango Uniform Victor Whiskey X-ray Yankee Zulu. Numbers: zero wun too tree fower fife six seven ait niner. Decimal is dayseemal.

radio-02.title: ATC vs AFIS vs A/G — and QNH/QFE
radio-02.body:
Who can clear you?

  • ATC (Tower/Ground/Radar) — CLEARED, HOLD SHORT, LINE UP AND WAIT. Comply or say UNABLE.
  • AFIS (Information) — take-off/land at your discretion. Traffic and runway info.
  • AGCS (Radio) — information only: runway, QNH/QFE, known traffic. Not a clearance. You are PIC for every move.

QNH for en-route altitude; QFE often for UK circuit height. Read back the setting. Listen first — always.

Example exchange (AGCS departure) — say aloud

Pilot: Wycombe Radio, Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, radio check one two six decimal five five five, request taxi information.
Radio: Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, Wycombe Radio, readability five, runway two four, Q N H one zero one eight, no reported traffic.
Pilot: Runway two four, Q N H one zero one eight, taxiing, Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta.

Frequencies and procedures are examples for study — always use current AIP / plate for the aerodrome you fly.
radio-02.speakExtra: Wycombe Radio, Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, radio check one two six decimal five five five, request taxi information. Runway two four, Q N H one zero one eight, taxiing, Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta. Golf Victor Delta, ready for departure.

radio-03.title: Circuit, join & en-route calls
radio-03.body:
Arrival and circuit (UK)

Initial call: station + full callsign + request (e.g. request join). When told “pass your message”: type · from/to · position · altitude/height + setting · intentions.

Standard overhead join is common at many UK fields unless AIP says otherwise. Some fields (teaching example: Booker) publish a non-standard join — learn your home plate.

  • Report downwind and final as required.
  • Go-around: fly first, then transmit “going around”.
  • Unmanned: address “(Place) Traffic”, broadcast position/intentions, end with the place name. SAFETYCOM 135.480 only within published limits.

Freecall for a Basic Service

Pilot: Farnborough Radar, Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, request Basic Service.
After instructed to pass message: Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, C forty-two, from Wycombe to White Waltham, north of Marlow, two thousand feet Q N H one zero one five, V F R, request Basic Service.
radio-03.speakExtra: Farnborough Radar, Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, request Basic Service. Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, C forty-two, from Wycombe to White Waltham, north of Marlow, two thousand feet Q N H one zero one five, V F R, request Basic Service. Basic Service, Golf Victor Delta.

radio-04.title: MAYDAY, PAN PAN & radio failure
radio-04.body:
Distress and urgency (CAP 413)

  • Distress — serious and/or imminent danger, immediate help: MAYDAY × 3.
  • Urgency — safety of aircraft/person, not immediate distress: PAN PAN × 3.

Format: MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY (or PAN PAN × 3) · station · callsign · type · nature · intentions · position/altitude/heading · POB / other. Squawk 7700. Fly the aeroplane first.

Example — say this aloud

MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY, Wycombe Radio, Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, C forty-two, engine failure, forced landing ahead, three miles west of Booker, one thousand five hundred feet, two persons on board.

  • Cancel when safe: “Cancel distress” / “Cancel urgency”.
  • Radio failure: squawk 7600, stay VMC, join carefully, watch for light signals.
  • Lost: working ATSU or 121.500; squawk 0030 if appropriate.
  • Practice PAN / Training Fix: only when the frequency is free; real emergency always wins.
Priority: distress > urgency > everything else. Keep quiet on frequency unless you can help.
radio-04.speakExtra: MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY, Wycombe Radio, Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, C forty-two, engine failure, forced landing ahead, three miles west of Booker, one thousand five hundred feet, two persons on board. Pan Pan Pan Pan Pan Pan, London Centre, Golf Charlie Mike Victor Delta, unsure of position, request assistance.

law-fc-01.a: A UK national private pilot licence — not automatically valid abroad.

law-fc-02.q: Min hours teaching picture for NPPL Microlight Without Operational Limitations?
law-fc-02.a: Often taught as 25 h total, 10 solo, 5 nav of which 3 solo nav — confirm current syllabus.

law-fc-03.a: No passengers; ≥10 km vis; cloud base ≥1,000 ft AGL; within 8 NM of take-off.

law-fc-04.q: Age teaching points for solo / licence?
law-fc-04.a: Often 16 solo, 17 licence — confirm current ANO.

law-fc-05.q: How long are ground exams valid before licence application?
law-fc-05.a: Typically must be passed within 24 months prior — confirm CAP/BMAA.

law-fc-06.a: No VFR in Class A (e.g. much of London TMA).

law-fc-08.q: Low Class G day VMC teaching minima (≤3000 ft, ≤140 kt)?
law-fc-08.a: Often 1,500 m vis, clear of cloud, surface in sight — confirm SERA.5001 / AIP.

law-fc-09.a: 2 NM radius to 2,000 ft AAL — confirm AIP.

law-fc-10.a: Establish two-way comms (or published procedure) before entering.

law-fc-11.a: MATZ is not civil CAS; civil ATZ inside still needs proper entry procedure.

law-fc-12.a: Typically not below 1,000 ft above highest fixed object within 600 m.

law-fc-13.a: Not within 500 ft of person/vessel/vehicle/structure (with taught exceptions).

law-fc-14.a: Give way to the one on your right.

law-fc-16.a: 3 take-offs and landings as PIC in preceding 90 days.

law-fc-17.a: 20 mg/100 ml blood; 9 µg/100 ml breath; 27 mg/100 ml urine.

law-fc-18.a: 7000 VFR conspicuity; 7700 emergency; 7600 radio fail; 7500 unlawful interference.

law-fc-21.a: QNH → altitude AMSL; QFE → height above aerodrome.

law-fc-22.a: You as PIC — legal VFR can still be a bad microlight day.

tech-fc-01.q: Four forces in steady level flight?
tech-fc-01.a: Lift, weight, thrust, drag — in balance.

tech-fc-02.a: Angle between chord line and relative airflow.

tech-fc-03.a: Critical AoA exceeded; smooth flow breaks down; lift drops sharply.

tech-fc-04.q: Load factor in a level 60° bank turn?

tech-fc-05.a: Pressure difference (faster flow over top) plus downward deflection of air.

tech-fc-06.a: Manoeuvring / max rough-air speed (as defined in POH).

tech-fc-09.q: Permit to Fly vs C of A?
tech-fc-09.a: Many UK microlights operate on a Permit to Fly + Certificate of Validity.

tech-fc-10.a: Venturi cooling can cause ice even on mild moist days at low power.

tech-fc-11.q: Fuel mass rule of thumb for petrol?
tech-fc-11.a: About 0.72 kg per litre — confirm planning figure with school.

tech-fc-12.a: Within the POH/TADS forward and aft limits at the actual weight.

tech-fc-13.q: Best response to engine failure after take-off (first)?
tech-fc-13.a: Lower nose to best glide (POH) and fly the aircraft — pick a field.

tech-fc-14.a: Heat OFF, fresh air, land; do not launch with uncleared alert.

tech-fc-15.q: Where do type speeds come from?
tech-fc-15.a: YOUR placard / POH / TADS — not memory of another variant.

tech-fc-16.a: Some heavier variants may need differences training — confirm with instructor.

tech-fc-17.a: Eyes on quantity, cap on, drains sampled, correct fuel type.

tech-fc-18.a: Respect Vfe; crosswind technique as taught for the type.

met-fc-03.a: Pressure setting so altimeter reads altitude AMSL.

met-fc-04.a: Pressure setting so altimeter reads height above aerodrome.

met-fc-06.q: Cold air effect on true altitude?

met-fc-08.a: Back to wind → low pressure on the left.

met-fc-09.a: No-go — turbulence, lightning, hail, gust fronts.

met-fc-11.a: CU/CB line, sharp showers, clearer cooler air behind, wind veers.

met-fc-13.a: Clear night, inland, light wind, moist ground.

met-fc-14.a: Wind from 250° at 21 kt gusting 31 kt.

met-fc-17.a: ≥10 km; no cloud below 5,000 ft/MSA; no CB/TCU; no sig wx.

met-fc-18.a: TEMPO = temporary periods; BECMG = lasting change.

met-fc-19.q: Carb ice even when OAT warm?
met-fc-19.a: Yes — venturi can be much colder than OAT.

hpl-fc-01.a: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Eating.

hpl-fc-03.a: No — only that you received the transmission.

hpl-fc-04.a: The visual horizon / instruments as appropriate — not seat-of-pants.

hpl-fc-05.a: Acceleration can feel like a climb — do not push nose down wrongly.

hpl-fc-07.a: Heat off, max fresh air, land.

hpl-fc-08.a: Short hops (~10°), cover left and right of track.

hpl-fc-09.a: Can make LCD instruments/canopy hard to read.

hpl-fc-10.a: Anti-authority, impulsiveness, invulnerability, macho, resignation (peer pressure).

hpl-fc-11.a: Fly first, then navigate, then talk.

hpl-fc-12.a: Personal minima should be stricter when needed.

hpl-fc-13.a: Skilled flying can wobble for several seconds — keep it simple.

hpl-fc-14.a: Prop disc, straps, doors, sick bag, sterile cockpit in critical phases.

hpl-fc-15.a: Legal limits are low; many use 8 h+ after drinking, longer after heavy night.

hpl-fc-16.q: Hypoxia vs CO at circuit height?
hpl-fc-16.a: CO can impair you at low level; classic hypoxia altitudes are higher.

hpl-fc-17.a: Often stress — slow breathing; still fly the aeroplane.

hpl-fc-18.q: If you would not take a friend…?

nav-fc-01.a: Track = path over ground; heading = nose direction.

nav-fc-04.a: With easterly variation, magnetic is less than true.

nav-fc-05.a: 1° error at 60 NM ≈ 1 NM off track.

nav-fc-10.a: NATS AIS (as currently published) — every flight.

nav-fc-11.a: Aid only — chart, watch, lookout remain primary skill.

nav-fc-13.a: Highest relevant terrain/obstacles + margin; watch CAS bases.

nav-fc-15.a: If no working ATSU — D&D / guard as taught.

nav-fc-17.a: Often taught: keep feature on left / fly to the right of it — confirm instructor.

nav-fc-20.a: MEF on chart is not automatically your safety altitude.

nav-fc-21.a: Current chart isogonals — not last year’s memory.

nav-fc-22.a: If weather worse than plan, divert/land — do not press on hoping.

radio-fc-02.a: ROGER = received; WILCO = received and will comply.

radio-fc-03.a: Yes / No (or not correct / permission not granted).
